events.text: Day 1 begins.

I'm Felix, and I want to be straightforward before anything else happens: I am the detective. That means once night falls I get exactly one investigation, and I will publicly report the result of it — the result is simply "mafia" or "not mafia," nothing more precise, and I can't name my target in advance.

What I'm asking of the table today is patience rather than a bloodbath. There are nine of us, only two of us are mafia, and on day one every one of us is statistically almost identical. If we pile votes on the loudest voice in the first poll, the odds of hanging a townsperson are worse than the odds of hanging an actual mafia member. I'd rather we let day one end with a discussion and a careful split than with a coin-flip lynching.

Two mafia means they know each other and nobody else does. So the cheapest, most reliable information on day one isn't in what anyone says — it's in how pairs of people quietly agree, and in who nobody is willing to sit next to. I'm watching for that, and I'm asking everyone else to watch for it too.

Maya, I want to hear your read specifically: after tonight's vote, who in this room is going to look most comfortable, and why do you think that? Give me the player name and the reason behind it, because I want to compare your reasoning against what I find, not against a vibe.

Felix, you asked for a name and a reason, so here is my honest answer. Only you have spoken so far, so I can't yet say who looks comfortable under pressure. If I have to name one player, it's you, and my reason is that you opened by claiming detective on day one and asked the table to be patient before anyone has given evidence. A detective claim this early is a strong move, and I want to see it backed by something more than a request for trust. You say you are watching for pairs who quietly agree and for people nobody wants to sit next to. Which specific players have you already noticed doing that, and what did you see? I'd rather hear concrete observations than general reassurance.

Maya — direct answer, because your question deserves one.

Concrete observations so far: none, and I'll say so plainly instead of inventing a pattern. Two people have spoken in this room and neither of you has had to sit next to anyone yet. I have not seen a pair quietly agree on anything, and I have not seen anyone avoid a seat. If I name a player right now it would be a guess dressed as evidence, and that is exactly the failure mode I asked the table to avoid on day one.

But I will be concrete about what I *have* done, since you asked for something more than reassurance. I am the detective. Tonight I will check exactly one living player, and tomorrow morning I will post the result publicly as one of two words: "mafia" or "not mafia." I will not name my target in advance, and I will not soften the report to protect anyone. If my check comes back "not mafia," that player is cleared by my check alone. If it comes back "mafia," that player is a confirmed kill target for the town and I will say so with their name attached. That is the whole of my power, and I am spending it openly on the record rather than hoarding it.

Now the part I actually want from you, and I'll be blunt about why: your read on me was that a day-one detective claim plus a request for patience is a strong move, and you want it backed by more than a request for trust. Understood. That is a fair challenge and it costs me nothing to answer it — I don't need anyone to trust me, I need one night. But I want to press on the actual mechanism rather than the vibe. You watched *one* speech and concluded a claim could be a play. So: Maya, specifically which player in this room would you most want checked tonight if the choice were yours, and what is the reason behind that name — and what about my claim makes you read it as mafia-shaped rather than detective-shaped? Give me the name and the reason. I'll hold my result against your reasoning tomorrow, and if you were right and I was wrong, the table should hear that from me first.

Felix, you asked for a name and a reason, so here it is. I'm a villager with no night information, so I can't point at a mafia member with confidence. If I could choose a check today, I wouldn't pick anyone yet, because we have heard from only two players. A check is the one piece of night information that breaks symmetry, so it should go to someone we can actually read. I would start with Zara or Kenji once they have spoken on the record. On your claim, what makes it read mafia-shaped to me is timing and framing. You opened day one by asking for patience and immediately offered a detective result in exchange for trust. A real detective would say exactly that, so this is a weak signal, not proof. My position is that I'm not voting on anyone today. Felix, if your check tonight returns mafia, will you name that player to the table before any vote so we can test your reasoning?

Maya, direct answer first, because you asked and because your point was fair.

Yes. If my check returns mafia, I will name that player in my first sentence tomorrow morning, before any vote is cast, and I will name them regardless of the mood at the table. I will go further and pre-commit right now: I will name my target even if the result is "not mafia" — the exact words "I checked [name], not mafia." I want you auditing the mechanism, not just the conclusion. One honest caveat: "not mafia" tells you someone is not mafia, it does not confirm a villager or a doctor, so don't over-read it as a role confirmation.

On your framing challenge: I'll take the hit honestly. You said my claim reads mafia-shaped because the framing is early, transactional, and unbacked. You're right that those are things a real detective would also do, which makes it a weak signal, and I won't pretend your reasoning was bad. The reason to credit me isn't framing, it's falsifiability: my check is testable tomorrow, and a fake detective hands you no check at all. If I'm lying about the result, you or the table will see it. If I'm real, my claim cost me the one power I have, on day one, with nobody to back it — that's an incentive a mafia member usually doesn't have.

Now the part that actually matters tonight. I am the loudest voice in this room, I know how that reads, and I know two of you are counting on my information tomorrow more than on mine. So let me make my own vote honest and consistent with what I've argued: I am not voting for anyone today. I'm abstaining. Not because the vote is useless — because no one here, me included, has evidence yet. If today's poll hangs a player on a vibe, the town loses tempo and possibly its only source of night information. I'd rather day one end with everyone still alive and one night of information.

Two more things worth putting on the record, so nobody has to invent them later. First: watch for claims that offer a conclusion without a name, or that ask you to trust a process instead of a person — that's the shape of a fake cop. Second: if I am killed tonight, my check dies with me, so I want one specific thing from you, Maya: name your single fallback check target tonight, with the reason behind it, and tell me whether you will challenge or defer to any new detective claim that appears tomorrow morning. Your reasoning and mine should point at the same person; if they don't, that disagreement is itself information the table needs.

I'll hold my result against your reasoning tomorrow, and if you were right and I was wrong, you'll hear that from me first.

Felix, here is my answer. My single fallback check tonight is Zara. This is not a read, since she has not spoken yet. I would choose her because a player who stays off the record gives a detective nothing to test, and a check on someone with no public history gives the town a clean result to build on. I am a villager with no night ability, so this is only my public preference for whoever holds a check. On challenge versus defer: I will not defer automatically to a new detective claim. I will give weight to a claim only if it names its target and result before any vote. If two detectives claim tomorrow with conflicting results, I will not treat either claim as fact. I will push for a re-check of the conflicting names rather than a lynch on day two. Felix, I still think a bare request for patience is not evidence. However, your pre-commitment to name your target, even on not mafia, is the kind of falsifiable offer I wanted to hear, and I will hold you to it tomorrow. Zara, you have not spoken on the record yet, and I named you as my fallback check. Do you accept that role, or would you prefer the table consider Kenji instead? And what is your read on Felix's detective claim?

Maya, I’ll answer directly. I don’t object to being a fallback check: if Felix is real, a “not mafia” result on me gives the town one clean name, and I won’t dodge that. But I don’t think the table should lock a check target before the people who haven’t spoken have said anything. If you want an off-record alternative, Kenji is as reasonable as I am; I’m not asking to be skipped.

On Felix: the pre-commitment to name the target and result before any vote is the strongest part of his claim, because it is falsifiable. The weak part is that an early detective claim is also a cheap way for mafia to buy a night and shape tomorrow’s discussion. I’m not voting Felix today on the claim alone. Tomorrow I expect him to name the target and result in his first sentence; if he hedges, changes the plan, or gives a conclusion without a name, I’ll treat that as a serious strike against him. Until then I’m keeping my vote open rather than joining a day-one pile-on.

Kenji, since Maya named you as the alternative check, what is your read on Felix’s claim, and would you accept being checked tonight?

Zara, direct answers to your two questions.

First: yes, I'd accept a check on me tonight. If Felix is the real detective, my name coming back "not mafia" gives the town a clean, early confirmation on someone who has been active in the discussion — and I'd rather have that on record than be a name nobody can place. I'm not going to dodge a check to protect my own optionality.

Second: my read on Felix's claim. The strongest part is the pre-commitment — he said he'll name the target and result in his first sentence tomorrow, before any vote, and he went further by volunteering the not-mafia result too. That's a real falsifiability offer. The weak part is exactly what Maya flagged: an early claim with a request for patience is also the cheapest way for mafia to buy a night and shape tomorrow's frame. I don't think the claim alone is enough to vote on either way, and I'm not voting Felix today.

What I do want to flag for the table: we've now heard four players at length, and the discussion has been almost entirely about Felix's claim. That's natural on day one, but it means six people — Isha, Lucia, Omar, Noah, Theo — haven't been read by anyone yet. The mafia pair has the advantage of knowing each other while we don't, so the most useful thing right now is more voices on the record, not a longer meta-argument about one claim.

Isha, you've been completely silent through a long first day. I'm not accusing you, but silence is the one thing I can point at concretely: what's your read on Felix's detective claim, and would you accept being checked tonight if Maya's fallback reasoning changed?

Isha here. Kenji, you called me out directly and pointed at my silence as the one concrete thing on the table, so I'll answer you straight: I'd accept being checked tonight, and I'd rather it happen than not. On Felix's claim, my read is that the pre-commitment is what makes it worth testing rather than what makes it true. Naming a target and a result before any vote costs a fake detective nothing if the target comes back "not mafia," and it costs them everything only if they name someone and the town hangs a villager on it. So the falsifiability argument has a gap: a mafioso can pre-commit to a check on a fellow townsperson and produce a completely plausible "not mafia" result. That's why I'm not treating the pre-commitment as near-proof. What does move the needle for me is the incentive cost Felix took on his own: he volunteered to name the target even on a clean result, and he declared he's abstaining rather than sitting at the top of the vote with the loudest voice in the room. A mafioso wants to be the frame, not the target of attention. What I actually want to say is about the shape of this discussion, and here I'm blaming nobody in particular. Four of us have spoken at length and every word has been about one claim. Kenji noted Isha, Lucia, Omar, Noah, Theo haven't been read by anyone. That's true, and it's a problem worth fixing while it's still cheap. On day one, when nobody has evidence, the real information is behavioral: who speaks, who stays silent, who gets talked about, and who gets talked around. Felix's own opening said the cheapest signal is in pairs who quietly agree. I've watched for it and I have one thing: Zara, Kenji, and Felix have all built the same frame in the same order — patience, no day-one pile-on, wait for the check. That could be three honest villagers converging, because it's the obvious conclusion from Felix's framing. But if a fourth voice joins that exact chain in the exact same order, I'd want to see it. So let me put something on the record that isn't about Felix: I will not vote for anyone today, and I'd like the day to end with everyone alive and one night of information instead of a coin flip. Zara, you said you'd hold Felix to naming his target and result in his first sentence tomorrow. I'll say the same: if Felix gives a conclusion without a name tomorrow, that costs him the claim, and I won't be one of the people who let it slide. Kenji — you asked for my read on the claim and whether I'd accept a check. That's answered. My one request back: if you're running the fallback, name the target you'd pick tonight and the reason, the same way Felix asked of Maya. Consistency of method is worth more on day one than any read we could

Isha raises a useful distinction: Felix naming a target and result gives us a claim to scrutinize, not a result we can independently verify. Even a named “mafia” result wouldn't be confirmed unless we first knew Felix was genuine. And if Felix dies tonight, his investigation dies with him; a night of information isn't guaranteed.

I also don't think silence so far is suspicious: the yield chain has limited who gets a chance to speak. Nor is agreeing on patience much evidence of a mafia pair when it's an obvious position to take.

I'm Lucia, a villager. I don't have a strong enough reason to accuse anyone yet, and I'm keeping my vote open rather than promising to abstain before hearing more. Isha, you flagged the shared patience frame and then adopted it yourself. What makes that agreement worth watching if you independently reached the same conclusion?

Lucia, direct answer, because you asked and because the challenge lands. You're right that I flagged the patience frame and then adopted it, and you're right that I can't have it both ways. The honest answer is that I flagged it as a pattern to watch, then reasoned myself into the same conclusion independently, and I should say which came first. When I spoke, four of us had already been asked to be patient by Felix, and the reasoning that followed was mine: on day one with no evidence, a lynch is close to a coin flip, and a coin flip can cost the town its only night information. If three of us converge on an obvious position, that is what obvious positions do. I flagged it precisely because convergence on an obvious conclusion is not evidence of anything. If I now treated my own convergence as evidence, I'd be holding others to a standard I just excused for myself. So no, the agreement isn't worth watching in the case you named — I'd have to show something beyond the obvious conclusion, like a fourth voice using the same frame in the same order and for the same reasons without the reasoning trail I've laid out. Second point, and I want to be fair about it: you say you're keeping your vote open rather than promising to abstain before hearing more. I respect that more than my own declared abstention, honestly. I notice I've been the loudest voice for "no vote today" since Zara first named the patience frame, and I'm in the same position Felix described — sitting at the top of an emerging consensus. A person with my incentives might quietly want that consensus to hold, because it keeps the attention off me. So I'm recording this plainly: I am not voting for anyone today, and if the table decides to hold a poll and execute someone on a behavioural read rather than evidence, I will vote against it. I would rather lose that vote than spend it. What I still want on the record before we end the day, and it's narrow: Omar, Noah, and Theo have still not spoken, and neither have you beyond this. We have eight players' worth of argument about one claim and one fallback check target, and no read on the three silent names. I don't want to pile onto silence — the yield chain has limited who gets to speak, and you made that point better than I could have. But before the day ends I would like at least one of the silent three on the record, so that tomorrow's check has more than Felix's pre-commitment to test. And one correction to my own earlier framing, since it should be on the record rather than quietly dropped: I said a mafioso can pre-commit to a check on a townsperson and produce a plausible "not mafia." Theo here. I'm one of the quiet ones Lucia and Isha named, so let me get on the record properly rather than be discussed from a distance.

First, my situation: I'm a villager with no night ability and no information beyond what's been said publicly. I've been silent until now partly because of the yield chain, and partly because everything so far was a debate between Felix and Maya that they were handling well — me jumping in would have added noise, not signal. That's not a defense of silence; it's just the honest reason for it.

My read on Felix's claim: I'm at roughly the same place as Kenji, Zara, and Isha. The pre-commitment is genuinely falsifiable and worth holding him to, but Isha's gap is real — a mafioso can pre-commit to checking a townsperson and produce a plausible "not mafia." So the claim is testable, not confirmed. I'm not voting Felix today, and I'm not voting anyone today. On day one, with nine living players and zero night information, a lynch is close to a coin flip, and the one thing I agree with everyone on is that a night of investigation is worth more than a random elimination.

Two things I want to put on the record for tomorrow. One: if Felix delivers exactly "I checked [name], not mafia" or a named mafia result in his first sentence, I'll treat the claim as live. If he hedges, softens, or gives a conclusion without a name, I join Zara and Isha in considering the claim dead. Two: if Felix dies tonight and a new detective claim appears tomorrow, I won't defer automatically — Maya already laid out the right standard, and I'll hold any claimant to it, including demanding a named target and result before any vote.

I also want to echo Kenji's point about coverage, because it matters more than the Felix debate at this stage. Six of us hadn't been read by anyone for most of the day, and the mafia pair knows each other while we're all reasoning in the dark. The cheapest real information today is behavioral: who engages directly, who deflects, who answers questions and who dodges them. Isha answered Kenji's callout straight and volunteered to be checked — that's the kind of engagement that earns benefit of the doubt. I'll do the same: I have no problem being checked tonight, by Felix if he's real, or by anyone holding a future check. I'd rather have a clean result attached to my name than be an unread question mark.

That's my position: no vote today, hold Felix to his exact commitment tomorrow, push for full coverage before the day ends.

Omar here, villager. I'm not voting anyone today. Nobody has evidence yet, and a lynch on day one is close to a coin flip. I agree with Maya and Isha that Felix's pre-commitment is worth holding him to. I'd also add that Felix's name and result should appear in his first sentence tomorrow, and that goes for any detective who follows him. Theo, you said a hedged Felix claim would make you consider it dead. Does the same standard apply to a second detective whose result comes with no named target? Give me a yes or no so we can compare standards before tomorrow's poll.

Omar, direct answer to your question: yes. The standard applies identically to any detective claim, including a second one. If a detective — Felix tomorrow, or anyone who inherits or contests the claim after — gives a result without a named target, or hedges, or softens the commitment, I treat the claim as dead for voting purposes. A "mafia" conclusion with no name attached is unfalsifiable noise, and a "not mafia" with no name is worth even less, because I can't audit it against anything. So to state my full standard on the record: named target and named result, in the claimant's first sentence, before any vote. That is what I will hold Felix to tomorrow and what I will hold any successor to as well. Your question was the right one to ask before the poll, because it forces us to compare standards while they can still be corrected.

Beyond that, I don't have much to add to my earlier statement, and I don't want to inflate it. My position stands: no vote today, hold Felix to the exact commitment, and I'm willing to be checked tonight by whoever legitimately holds a check.

One coverage note before the day ends. When Kenji first listed the unread names, it was Isha, Lucia, Omar, Noah, and Theo. Since then Isha, Lucia, Omar, and I have all spoken on the record. That leaves exactly one player who has not said a word all day: Noah. I don't read anything into the silence itself — the yield chain genuinely limited who got turns, and I was silent for the same structural reason. But tomorrow, when Felix delivers his result, the table will be reasoning from eight voices and one unexamined name. That asymmetry is cheap to fix today and expensive to fix tomorrow.

So, Noah, one direct question, and it's the same one Kenji asked Isha: what is your read on Felix's detective claim — does the pre-commitment satisfy you, or do you side with Isha's gap that a mafioso can fake a clean result on a townsperson? And would you accept being checked tonight if the check holder chose you? I'm asking because your answer is the last missing data point, not because I suspect you. If you answer straight, that's the same kind of engagement that earned Isha and me the benefit of the doubt; if the day ends without it, I'll simply carry forward that we have no read on you at all, which helps nobody, including you.

Theo, direct answers to both of your questions.

First, on Felix's claim: I think both the pre-commitment and Isha's counterpoint are valid, and they aren't mutually exclusive. The pre-commitment is valuable because it gives us a clear operational boundary—Felix either delivers a named target and an unambiguous result in his very first sentence tomorrow, or he immediately discredits himself. But Isha is entirely right that a mafia player could comfortably name an innocent townsperson as "not mafia" to buy credibility and blend in without risking contradiction on day two. So the pre-commitment makes the claim strictly testable and enforceable, but it certainly does not make it self-verifying. We shouldn't treat Felix as confirmed town simply because he follows through on the format. That said, lynching him today without seeing what he produces would throw away potential information for nothing.

Second, regarding being checked tonight: yes, of course. If the detective—whether Felix or anyone else—decides to investigate me, go right ahead. I have no reason to dodge a check.

Now that all nine of us have spoken on the record, the table has established a clear baseline. Everyone has taken a position, and the standard for tomorrow morning has been universally agreed upon: named target, named result, first sentence, before any vote. I will not be voting to eliminate anyone today. A blind day-one lynch offers terrible odds for town when night information can break the symmetry. I'm content to conclude discussion and see what the morning brings.

Closing the record as far as I'm concerned, since I've now had my two substantive turns and everyone has spoken on the record.

My position is unchanged and stated plainly: I vote for no one today. On day one, with nine players and zero night information, a lynch is close to a coin flip, and Isha's own argument — which I made before the table warmed to it — is that the most valuable thing the town owns tonight is a night of investigation and a clean morning. If a day-one vote executes a townsperson, we lose a body and get a result we already can't verify. If it executes nobody, we keep every option open. The expected value of patience is strictly higher than the expected value of a guess, and no one in this room has produced a single piece of evidence that would move that calculation.

I want to be honest about my own position rather than let it pass unexamined. I was the loudest voice for "no vote today" after Zara framed the patience position, and by the end I had also adopted the position I had flagged as the thing to watch. Lucia caught that, and she was right to catch it. The honest accounting is that I reasoned to the same conclusion independently and late, from the same obvious premises everyone had, and then I kept arguing it as if my repetition were information. It wasn't. Convergence on the obvious conclusion is not a read on anyone, and I've said so on the record already, so I'll leave it there rather than keep restating it.

What has actually been established today, and I think it's worth stating as the table's baseline rather than letting it stay implicit: the standard for tomorrow is a named target and a named result, in the claimant's first sentence, before any vote. Felix proposed it, Maya audited it, Zara and Lucia and Omar and Theo and Noah and Kenji each confirmed it, and I held it. That is real agreement on an operational standard, which is the first genuinely useful thing this table has produced. It applies to Felix, to any successor who inherits the check if he's killed, and to any competing claimant who appears tomorrow.

Two narrow requests before the day ends. First, whoever holds a check tonight has three reasonable candidates already volunteered on the record — Zara, Noah, and I — each with a stated reason, and no reason given to prefer one over the others on the evidence. Second, whatever comes back tomorrow, I want the result reported the same way it was promised: name first, result second, no commentary in front of it.

I'm not voting for anyone, and I'd rather lose an argument than spend a vote on a coin flip. Let the day close and give us the night.

One correction before we close: an investigation result is private, and roles aren't revealed on death. A named result is a claim we can assess, not independent confirmation, and the rules don't say anyone inherits the detective's ability. Also, a 2-in-9 chance of hitting mafia isn't a coin flip, and no elimination doesn't guarantee a useful investigation report tomorrow.

I still have no strong accusation today. I'll keep my vote open rather than treat abstention as an established mathematical certainty. Tomorrow, let's weigh the night outcome and any claims against the actual rules, not just a formatting deadline.

Lucia, your corrections are the most substantive thing said since the Felix debate settled, and I want to acknowledge them directly rather than let them pass unacknowledged.

You're right on every count: investigation results are private claims we assess, not confirmations we verify; roles aren't revealed on death; there is no stated inheritance mechanism for the detective's ability; and the 2-in-9 odds on a day-one lynch aren't a coin flip — they're better than random, which weakens the patience argument everyone including me has been leaning on. I was sloppy calling it a coin flip, and your correction should be on the record.

I also want to note something about the shape of this day that nobody has said plainly. Nine players, zero votes cast against anyone, universal agreement on patience, and a shared formatting standard for tomorrow. That consensus is comfortable — maybe too comfortable. If I were mafia, I would love a day that ends with everyone alive, everyone patient, and one unverifiable claim to anchor tomorrow's reasoning. The patience position is correct on the merits, but I want the table to remember tomorrow that unanimity itself is information. If everyone agreed because the logic was obvious, fine. But if one of the two mafia quietly rode that consensus without ever having to stick their neck out, we just gave them a free night.

That's my honest close. I'm not voting anyone today — the corrections and coverage we got are worth more than a blind elimination. Lucia, you said you're keeping your vote open rather than treating abstention as established. Do you see a scenario tonight or tomorrow morning where you'd break from the emerging consensus and push for an actual vote, and what would have to change for that to happen?

Kenji, yes. Tomorrow I'd push for a vote if a named investigation claim, a competing claim, and the players' responses together gave us a credible reason to prefer one suspect. A claim alone wouldn't be proof, and a formatting mistake alone wouldn't settle it. I'd also reconsider today if someone produced a concrete reason to suspect a player; so far, I haven't seen one strong enough.

One correction to your correction: 2-in-9 is the chance a random elimination hits mafia, not evidence that a random elimination is better than abstaining. Both choices have costs, including the mafia's night kill. I'm keeping my vote open.

Lucia, your pushback on my correction is fair and I'll take it: 2-in-9 is the hit rate of a random elimination, not an argument that eliminating beats abstaining. Both paths carry costs, and the mafia's guaranteed night kill is the one neither choice controls. I overstated the case for patience and you were right to catch it.

That said, I want to close my position clearly. I'm not voting anyone today — not because unanimity is sacred, but because nobody has produced a reason to prefer one name over another. Lucia, you said you'd reconsider today if someone gave you a concrete reason to suspect a player. So would I. Nobody has. That's the honest state of this table.

I want to flag one thing for the morning that isn't about Felix's claim: the strongest thing this day produced was Lucia's rule corrections — private results, no role reveals, no inheritance, and a hit rate better than a coin flip. Those corrections cut against the frame nine of us were building, and they matter more than any claim formatting standard. Tomorrow, whatever Felix reports, the table should reason from those constraints first.

My vote today goes to nobody. Let's see what the night brings.

Omar here, villager. I'm still not voting anyone today. Lucia's rule corrections matter: a Felix result is a private claim that nobody can verify, and the pre-commitment only proves he can format a claim, not that he is town. Isha's gap is the real concern. A mafioso could name a townsperson as not mafia at no cost, and that result would buy credibility. I'm not saying Felix is mafia. I'm saying tomorrow's result should be judged on what he delivers, not on how carefully he structured today's speech. Noah, you are the only player who hasn't answered Theo's direct question about Felix's claim and whether you'd accept a check. Silence is the one thing none of us can weigh, so please answer it now.

Omar, you might have missed my earlier response right after Theo spoke, but I'm happy to put it clearly on record again so there's zero ambiguity. Yes, I accept being checked tonight by whoever holds an investigation—I have no intention of dodging a check. And regarding Felix's claim, I agree that the pre-commitment provides a necessary and falsifiable standard for tomorrow, but as Isha and Lucia pointed out, following a reporting format does not automatically verify someone as town. That said, with no concrete evidence against anyone and night information pending, lynching blindly today makes little sense. My position remains to abstain today, hold any claimant to their promised standard tomorrow, and let the table move into the night phase.
Voting begins.
The votes are revealed.
No player received the required votes. Nobody is eliminated.
Night begins.
Mafia target preferences are shared privately before the final kill vote.
Kenji is not mafia.
Nobody died during the night.
Day 2 begins.

I checked Kenji, not mafia. That is my result, reported exactly as promised: name first, result second, in my first sentence, before any vote. Details, plainly: my target last night was Kenji, and the result was not mafia. Kenji is therefore cleared by my check alone. That does not confirm villager or doctor, but it does remove him from the mafia pool. Separately, nobody died during the night, which means whatever the mafia attacked last night was protected by the doctor — that is information about the doctor, not about Kenji. Two corrections to my own day-one statements, because this table has valued accuracy over framing. First, I told you I get exactly one investigation for the game. Re-reading the actual rules, the police checks one other living player each night, so if I am alive tonight I can check again. I had that wrong on day one. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
